title: Service Decomposition
html:
Service Decomposition

In Chapter 10, we treated each deployment as a controlled experiment that one team could run, evaluate, and reverse on its own. That approach assumes a team can release its change without waiting for another team, and at Baodium the assumption failed in an unexpected place. Two days after a checkout outage, the Catalog team reopened its request to add a column to the products table, and the Checkout team replied in the review thread asking to approve every future change to that table. The Catalog team answered that the table was theirs. Both positions were reasonable, and together they described the problem this chapter addresses: one table, two teams with a legitimate interest in it, and no agreed rule for who could change it.

The shared ownership followed from Baodium’s original architecture. Baodium started as one Rails application maintained by five engineers. Catalog, Checkout, and Inventory code ran in the same application against the same database, so when a feature needed information from another part of the product, an engineer could call a function or join another table, and related updates could commit in one transaction. For a team of five, that arrangement made development fast and simple.

By the time Baodium had about forty engineers and 800,000 products, several capabilities had their own processes, repositories, and deployment pipelines, and some had been rewritten in other languages, including the Python services used in earlier chapters. Catalog and the checkout application, implemented by Order Service, could release code independently, but Order Service continued to query Catalog’s product tables directly. In this chapter, Checkout refers to the business capability and Order Service to the running service that implements it. Separate repositories and pipelines had not removed the data dependency between them, so a schema change could block both services.

A merchandising change exposed the consequence when the Catalog team added display_weight, a nullable column in products, and populated it from existing merchandising data. The migration had passed review and completed in staging, but in production, the migration tool ran the table alteration and the backfill in one transaction. PostgreSQL acquired an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the alteration and held it until the transaction committed, which meant holding it for the entire backfill. Order Service queried products during order acceptance to check whether cart items were eligible for sale, those reads waited behind the lock, database calls began reaching their deadlines, and customers could no longer complete affected checkouts. The lock was released when the migration committed about thirty minutes later, after which reads resumed and requests that had timed out went through their normal retry or recovery handling.

The immediate remedy was to separate the schema alteration from the backfill. That removed the long lock while preserving the existing architecture. A lasting change required the teams to decide who could modify product records, which information Checkout needed during order acceptance, and whether those dependencies justified a separate data store. Any extraction would also introduce network failure, migration steps, and ongoing operational responsibilities.

Fixing the Migration First

The direct cause of the outage was the migration procedure, and fixing it required no new service or database. Adding a nullable column without a default is a fast change in PostgreSQL, because it updates only the table’s metadata, and the exclusive lock it needs lasts milliseconds. The problem was that the backfill ran inside the same transaction, so the lock was held until the backfill finished. Committing the column addition on its own, and then populating values in small batches while application code accepts rows whose new value is not yet populated, keeps the exclusive lock to a moment. The backfill consumes database CPU, row locks, and I/O in its own right, so its rate needs to be tested alongside ordinary traffic.

The migration also needed a limit on how long it would wait for its lock. An ALTER TABLE that waits behind a long-running query blocks every query that arrives after it, even before it acquires the lock, so a migration waiting indefinitely can cause an outage of its own. Setting lock_timeout to a few seconds before the alteration makes the migration give up and fail cleanly if the lock is unavailable, and the team can retry it during a period of lower traffic rather than blocking production while it waits.

The responder’s options during an incident also needed to be clear. Identifying the blocking transaction is the first step, but stopping it takes care, because canceling a statement with pg_cancel_backend inside an explicit transaction leaves the transaction open and its locks held until the client rolls it back. Terminating the session with pg_terminate_backend ends the transaction and releases its locks immediately, at the cost of discarding its uncommitted work.

These changes improved the existing system whether or not Catalog ever received its own database. They did not answer the broader question, however, which was whether Order Service should read Catalog’s tables at all. A better migration leaves open who may change those tables, which consumers depend on them, and what Checkout should do when product information is unavailable.

Release, Runtime, and Data Boundaries

Extracting a service can change several arrangements at once, and each one solves its own class of problem. Figure \(\ref{fig:ch11-coupling}\) separates three kinds of coupling inside one application, and Figure \(\ref{fig:ch11-boundary}\) shows what splitting into services removes and what it leaves in place.

Table \(\ref{tab:decomposition-boundaries}\) lists the four separations that an extraction can provide, together with the dependencies each one leaves to examine.

Each separation stops one form of interference and leaves the others. Separate processes prevent a Catalog crash from terminating Order Service, but they do not prevent Catalog’s queries from consuming shared database capacity. Separate schemas and database roles can enforce ownership on a single database server, which may be all the protection a team needs against unauthorized writes and undocumented table access, although both domains then share the server’s CPU, I/O, and maintenance operations. Dedicated database instances separate those resources as well, but each instance needs its own capacity planning, backups, restoration tests, credentials, and operational support, so the benefit has to justify those responsibilities.

The Modular Monolith

A single application can enforce useful boundaries before any network call is introduced. A Catalog module can own product data and expose operations to other modules, and Checkout can use those operations without importing Catalog’s persistence code or writing its own product queries, with dependency checks and tests enforcing the arrangement. This arrangement, often called a modular monolith, keeps local calls and transactions while making unauthorized dependencies easy to detect. It is also the cheapest place to discover whether a boundary is in the right position, because inside one codebase a violation is a failed build and a refactor is a single commit, whereas across a network the same violation becomes a production incident.

For an application whose responsibilities are being worked out, a modular monolith is often the better choice. Extracting a service becomes more attractive when a specific requirement calls for independent deployment, a separate resource allocation, restricted access, or a distinct operating owner. At Baodium, Catalog already had a team and a release process of its own, so the remaining work concerned its consumers and the question of who had authority over its data.

Domain Ownership

A database table is an implementation detail, and assigning one to a service should start with the decisions its records support. For each record, the useful questions are who makes the decision it supports, what information that decision requires, and how current that information must be. The answers usually place the line between services more accurately than the schema does. At Baodium, the product-related information served the purposes shown in Table \(\ref{tab:product-ownership}\).

The table shows that the word product names two distinct records. Catalog owns a listing that merchants can edit, reprice, and retire, whereas Checkout needs the product details the customer accepted when placing the order, even if the listing changes later. Editing a product title should not rewrite the description on an existing order, so Checkout records the relevant description and accepted terms when the order is created, and Catalog continues to maintain the current listing. Keeping those records separate has a second benefit, which is that customers can view their past purchases even when Catalog is unavailable.

Domain-driven design calls the area within which a term has one agreed meaning a bounded context. Recognizing that Catalog and Checkout are separate contexts tells the engineers which information Checkout can copy and which operations must go through Catalog. Team responsibilities follow the same lines, so Catalog’s owner is responsible for its contracts, schema, capacity, and recovery. If every internal change to Catalog needs several teams to approve it, the team examines which dependency is forcing that coordination rather than accepting it as the price of working together.

Transaction Boundaries

The proposed split needs the closest examination wherever a single transaction currently enforces a business rule. Inventory, for instance, creates a reservation and reduces available quantity in one local transaction, and splitting those two updates across services would require a protocol for the case in which one commits and the other fails. Baodium avoided that by defining reservation as a single Inventory operation. Checkout requests a reservation, rather than reading a quantity and later sending a separate decrement, so the rule remains enforced inside one transaction owned by one service.

Catalog’s sale-eligibility check needed similar care, because reading that a product was sellable immediately before confirming an order did not prevent a merchant from withdrawing the product between the read and the order commit, and replacing the read with an API call would not close that gap. A response from the responsible service is authoritative, but it does not form an atomic transaction with the caller’s commit. The engineers and the product owner therefore had to decide when an eligibility decision became binding. One contract could let a decision remain valid for a specified operation until an expiry time, accepting that a product withdrawn in that window might be sold anyway. Another could require that a withdrawal prevent every later acceptance, including orders already in progress, which needs a reservation-like operation or keeping the decision and the order commit under one owner. Settling that requirement before the extraction mattered, because discovering a missing correctness rule after two databases already accept independent writes is far more expensive to fix.

::: decision

**Extract, or fix the boundary in place?**

Checkout reads Catalog’s products table directly. A Catalog migration has already halted checkout once. The team is considering four responses, and has roughly one quarter of engineering time available.

**Give the existing Catalog service its own database and replace Checkout’s direct table access with the Catalog contract.**

**Keep one database, but revoke Checkout’s table access and put a Catalog-owned interface in front of it.**

**Keep direct access and require migrations to run in small, non-blocking steps.**

**Copy the fields Checkout needs into Checkout’s own tables.**

—

C addresses the migration’s immediate locking behavior by separating the schema change from the backfill and testing bounded batches, but direct table access leaves Checkout coupled to Catalog’s schema.

B replaces that direct access with a Catalog-owned contract, so Catalog can change its implementation while preserving the contract. Both services can be delayed by locks and resource contention in the shared database, however, even though they no longer share an application connection pool.

A separates database ownership and can reduce that contention, but it adds a network call, availability requirements for the Catalog service, and a data migration. Shared infrastructure and synchronous dependencies need explicit failure handling, and an interface already established under B makes the later extraction easier.

D gives Checkout a local projection for reads that can tolerate its update delay. A purchase decision that requires current sale eligibility needs an authoritative check or another contract that preserves that requirement.

Correct the migration first, then choose B, A, or D according to the independent changes and read guarantees the teams need. A quarter of engineering time is a planning constraint, not evidence that any option will fit without an implementation estimate.

:::

Consumer Contracts

Order Service queried Catalog’s schema to decide whether each cart item could be accepted for sale, so the replacement contract needed to return that decision without exposing Catalog’s internal columns. A generic endpoint that returned every product field would leave Order Service interpreting Catalog’s internal state, which recreates the original coupling over HTTP. A bounded assessment operation instead accepts the cart’s product references and returns an explicit result for each item. An unknown product, an ineligible product, and an assessment that could not be completed are separate results, because a timeout is not evidence that a product does not exist.

Request cost needs the same attention, because replacing one SQL query with one network request per cart line would add many calls to every order acceptance, so the operation takes the whole cart in one batch, with a maximum batch size and a defined result for items whose assessment did not complete. Authorization also has to work across the new boundary. A service identity establishes which application is calling, while tenant and user rules determine which records it may access on a customer’s behalf.

Required Synchronous Decisions

If Order Service requires a current Catalog assessment before accepting an order, a Catalog outage prevents new orders from being accepted, even after Catalog has its own database, and a migration that blocks Catalog’s assessment query affects checkout through the API instead of through the table. Extraction removes direct schema access and lets Catalog control its queries, admission, and responses, and Order Service can bound the call with the deadlines and concurrency limits from earlier chapters, but the business dependency remains. The availability claims for the extraction must reflect that distinction. Historical orders can be displayed from stored order details, whereas new orders that need Catalog’s current decision receive the agreed unavailable or deferred response. A circuit breaker can contain resource use during a Catalog outage, but it cannot supply the missing business decision.

Local Copies

The alternative to calling the owner on every request is to keep a local copy, which is called a projection when one service maintains it from another service’s changes. A projection suits consumers that can tolerate delayed updates. A browsing page can show a new description a few seconds late, and a projection of stock levels can support display while actual reservations go through Inventory. Sale eligibility may need stricter treatment than descriptive text, because each consumer’s use of the information sets its freshness requirement.

Every projection needs a permitted freshness interval, evidence that updates are being processed, and a defined response when that evidence is missing. The time since a product last changed is not that evidence, because a product that has not changed in months can be perfectly current. The consumer needs to know how far it has progressed through the source’s change history, including periods in which no relevant product changed.

Incremental Extraction

Baodium improved the contract before transferring any data, following the three stages in Figure \(\ref{fig:ch11-stages}\), each of which removes one kind of sharing.

Replacing one caller’s direct table access at a time is often called the strangler pattern, after the strangler fig, a vine that grows around a tree and gradually takes over its structure. Its advantage is that each step is small and reversible, so a mistake affects one caller rather than the whole system. For Order Service’s eligibility query, Baodium used nine steps, each with a check that had to pass before the next began.

  1. Local adapter. Place Order Service’s product SQL behind a CatalogClient interface inside Order Service, which continues to query the shared tables. Check: no product-table SQL remains outside the adapter.

  2. Contract operations. Redesign the adapter’s operations while they are local calls and inexpensive to change. One cart assessment replaced ten per-item lookups before any network round trip existed.

  3. Contract tests. Catalog publishes the assessment schema and item-level results, and Order Service’s tests run against it. Check: an incompatible Catalog change fails Catalog’s build.

  4. Remote endpoint. Catalog serves the assessment from its own process, initially reading the same shared tables.

  5. Shadow comparison. The adapter calls both implementations, returns the local result, and records any mismatch. Check: over seven days, which included the weekly price import, mismatches remained below one per 100,000 assessments, and each had a known cause.

  6. Selected callers. Route 1, then 10, then 100 percent of assessments to the remote endpoint, applying the unavailable-result policy from the dependency inventory.

  7. Revoke table permission. Remove the Order Service role’s access to Catalog’s tables.

  8. Transfer data ownership. Transfer Catalog’s tables to its own database, as described in Section \(\ref{sec:ch11-authority}\).

  9. Delete the compatibility path. Remove the local implementation and the shadow code from Order Service.

The order of these steps matters, because redesigning the operations in step 2, while they are function calls, lets the team fix a chatty interface before it costs a network round trip per item, and the shadow comparison in step 5 proves that the remote endpoint gives the same answers before any customer depends on it. Step 7 is the one that proves the boundary exists, because until the permission is gone, a forgotten report, script, or code path can read the tables, and the inventory of consumers remains a claim rather than a fact. Listing \(\ref{lst:ch11-revoke}\) shows the revocation and the check that confirms it.

[
  language=SQL,
  caption={Revoking the checkout role's product-table access, then
           confirming it.},
  label={lst:ch11-revoke}]
REVOKE SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
  ON products, product_prices, product_eligibility
  FROM order_service;

-- Expected result: false for every table
SELECT has_table_privilege('order_service', 'products', 'SELECT');

The team revoked the permission first in staging and then in production, during business hours, with the previous grant script ready to run, and watched for permission errors from every role. A permission error from an unexpected job identified a dependency that the inventory had missed. Because Catalog already ran as its own process, step 4 added an endpoint rather than a new service, and most of the effort went into steps 5 through 8.

Dependency Inventory

Searching the code identified many readers and writers, but not all of them. The engineers also reviewed database activity, service accounts, scheduled jobs, reporting tools, imports, administrative scripts, foreign keys, and recovery procedures, and recorded a replacement and an owner for each dependency, as in Listing \(\ref{lst:ch11-inventory}\).

[
  caption={An example entry in the Catalog dependency inventory.},
  label={lst:ch11-inventory}
]
Consumer: checkout
Current access: SELECT from products
Purpose: eligibility during order acceptance
Replacement: bounded Catalog assessment operation
Unavailable result: acceptance deferred or refused by contract
Owner: checkout team
Retirement evidence: direct table access is denied

Runtime evidence needs an observation period that matches the workload, because a monthly report will not show up in one day of query logs, and configuration review and conversations with owners fill the gaps that observation misses. Separate database roles for each application made this work possible. With shared credentials, nobody can tell which application issued a query or what else will break when access is revoked, whereas with one role per application, every query is attributable and access can be removed selectively. New cross-domain writes were prohibited during the migration, because otherwise the engineers could finish replacing one dependency while another team introduced a new one.

Data Authority Transfer

Transferring Catalog’s tables to its own database creates a period in which two databases hold the same records, and the plan has to state which one is authoritative for each record at every moment. The destination needs every existing product record, every update accepted while the copy is in progress, and a single, unambiguous point at which Catalog begins writing to it. Writing to both databases independently during the transfer would introduce a failure between the two commits, so Baodium kept one authoritative source throughout and copied and synchronized the destination from it.

Snapshot and Change Capture

The transfer began with a consistent snapshot tied to a known position in PostgreSQL’s change log, and every change after that position was captured and applied to the destination. The snapshot and the change stream had to cover the source history without a gap. Exporting a table first and starting change capture afterward could miss writes committed during the export, which is why the snapshot and the starting position of the change stream were taken together.

Verification covered updates and deletions as well as inserts, and the engineers checked indexes, constraints, permissions, and identifier-generator state separately, because the replication mechanism did not necessarily reproduce them. Matching row counts can hide incorrect values, so the comparison also covered aligned key ranges and business properties such as tenant ownership, product identity, and required relationships. Each comparison used a known synchronization position or consistent snapshots on both sides, because comparing two changing databases at unrelated moments can make replication delay look like a conversion error.

Change capture also needed monitoring, because a logical replication slot keeps the source’s change log until the destination confirms it has applied the changes, so if the destination stops applying them, the retained log grows and can fill the production database’s storage. The plan therefore included a limit on that backlog and a procedure for pausing or abandoning the transfer. Throughout synchronization, the source continued to accept authoritative writes, and reads from the destination were tested only where their freshness contract allowed it, while decisions that required current data kept using the source.

Write Cutover

For the final switch, the team chose a brief pause in product updates rather than a more elaborate live cutover, because a pause makes the final state much easier to verify and merchants could tolerate a few minutes without editing listings. Reads continued wherever their contract permitted, and the cutover followed six steps.

  1. Stop admitting new writes through every legacy write path.

  2. Complete or abort active source write transactions, and prevent old processes from starting new ones.

  3. Record the final source change position after those transactions have ended.

  4. Apply destination changes through that position, and verify the required data and constraints.

  5. Enable destination writes through Catalog, and direct approved writers to it.

  6. Verify that attempts through legacy write paths are refused.

Changing credentials does not stop transactions that are already running, so the fencing in step 2 covers existing sessions, pooled connections, scheduled jobs, and privileged tools. The final position is recorded only after those writers have stopped, because a destination reported as caught up a moment earlier may lack the last accepted update.

The direction of recovery depends on where the cutover stands. Before destination writes begin, a failed verification can return control to the source without loss. After Catalog accepts writes at the destination, the source is an outdated copy unless verified reverse synchronization exists, and redirecting writes back to it would require another full transfer of authority, because otherwise accepted changes could be lost or two conflicting histories created. The team rehearsed failures at each step so that a responder would always know which database was authoritative and which recovery action was permitted.

Legacy Retirement

Consumers lost direct table access once they had adopted the Catalog contract, and the source copy was kept under restricted access for the agreed verification and retention period, so that no application could fall back on it informally. Historical orders kept their accepted details and product references, and Catalog’s deletion policy accounted for those references, so that retiring a listing never made a past order impossible to interpret. Reporting consumers received approved analytical copies or exports instead of operational access, because unrestricted access for reporting tools would create new schema dependencies outside the contract.

Event-Driven Projections

Once Catalog controlled its own writes, it could publish changes for search, browsing, and other consumers that accept delayed updates. Each of those consumers keeps a projection that stores only what it needs, in a form suited to its own queries, so search might keep descriptions and categories while another consumer keeps only product identity and display attributes. Before building a projection, the team assigns responsibility for detecting differences from the source and repairing missing or outdated records, because without that responsibility a projection drifts silently.

Catalog commits each business update and its outbox record in one transaction, and the consumer commits each projection update and its processing marker in one local transaction. The order of those two writes matters, because if the consumer committed the marker before the update, a crash between the two would leave the event marked as processed without changing the projection, and redelivery would then skip it. Duplicate detection also leaves ordering unsolved, because two separate events for the same product can arrive in the wrong order, so each event includes a source version, and the consumer ignores any event older than the version it has already applied.

Each consumer also needs freshness monitoring, handling for records that fail to apply, and a rebuild procedure, because a projection reduces the synchronous dependency only for the operations and the delay that its contract permits. Chapter 12 examines delivery, ordering, and replay in detail. Not every relationship has to begin as a synchronous call and become asynchronous later, however, and a consumer can use events from the start once ownership and its processing contract are established.

Extraction Cost and Order

Every additional service needs deployment, capacity management, credentials, telemetry, recovery procedures, and an operating owner. Its callers take on network failures and compatibility obligations, and any copied data needs repair and reconciliation, all of which continue long after the migration project ends. The question to ask before an extraction is therefore whether its benefit justifies an owner, an on-call rotation, and a contract maintained for years, rather than whether the result looks cleaner.

A service with a small codebase can be expensive to run independently, especially when every feature requires coordinated deployments across several services. The term distributed monolith describes that condition, in which separately running applications remain tightly coupled, but the useful diagnosis names the specific mechanism. At Baodium, direct table access prevented independent schema changes. In another system, a shared library might force simultaneous upgrades, or a chain of synchronous calls might make one customer operation depend on the availability of many services. Some coordination reflects a genuine business requirement, and the engineers keep that requirement while questioning dependencies that serve no current purpose.

The Next Extraction

Baodium compared candidates for the next extraction by the operating benefit, the migration work, and the consequence of stopping partway. Catalog had an established owner and many read consumers, and extracting it removed direct schema dependencies, although sale eligibility needed an explicit contract. Inventory reservations justified keeping reservation identity and quantity changes in one local transaction. Notification work could run after order acceptance, provided the obligation to deliver was recorded durably, and financial operations required the identity and recovery procedures from Chapter 3. A tightly interleaved pricing and discount calculation would gain more from a cleaner internal module than from a separate process. Choosing the next service this way, rather than by table count or code size, means the team selects a benefit it can demonstrate and recovery work it can support.

Boundary Verification

An extraction needs tests that demonstrate the result it was meant to produce. For Catalog, the first check was that Order Service’s database role could no longer read or write product tables. The engineers then exercised the replacement contract with Catalog unavailable, delayed, and returning explicit item-level results. Historical orders continued to display from stored details, and new orders that required a Catalog assessment followed their unavailable or deferred policy, with a fast rejection counted as a failed checkout rather than a successful one.

A migration rehearsal then blocked the relevant Catalog query and confirmed the same behavior, which kept the team from assuming that a dedicated database had removed the synchronous business dependency. Cutover tests confirmed that the destination contained the final accepted source changes, that legacy writes were refused, and that no tested failure could leave both databases accepting authoritative writes. Projection tests paused processing, checked the response to stale data, and rebuilt a copy using the approved procedure.

The engineers also checked ordinary development, which is where the extraction’s value shows. Could Catalog change an internal table without deploying Order Service? Did contract tests catch an incompatible response? Could each team diagnose its part of a failed request without unrestricted access to the other team’s database? The answers showed what the extraction had achieved and which coordination requirements remained.

Summary

The Catalog migration blocked checkout because two independently deployed services relied on the same product table. Splitting the schema alteration from the backfill removed the immediate locking hazard. It did not resolve who could change the table or which data Checkout needed during order acceptance.

The teams first clarified authority over products, accepted orders, and inventory reservations. Checkout could retain the order details required to explain an accepted purchase, while new purchases still needed a current eligibility assessment from Catalog. Replacing direct table access with a service contract made that dependency explicit. Moving Catalog data to a separate database then required a staged migration, compatibility rules, and tests for the period when old and new paths operated together. Some consumers could instead receive local projections, accepting a documented delay between a Catalog update and their own view.

A service extraction is justified by the coordination or failure boundary it changes. When a safer migration procedure, a module contract, or restricted table access resolves the immediate problem, a new network boundary may add more operating work than it removes. Chapter 12 follows the asynchronous projections introduced here and examines what happens when their events are duplicated, delayed, or received out of order.

::: hiddenassumptions

Assumption and scope & Separate application deployments allow Catalog and Checkout to change independently while both access the product table.
Condition that tests it & A Catalog schema change or failure interrupts checkout, or a shared table or release forces the teams to coordinate.
Constraint or invariant & Catalog controls product writes and consumer contracts, Checkout owns accepted order details, Inventory owns reservation transactions, and database permissions enforce those responsibilities.
Evidence and uncertainty & Verification confirms that direct table access is removed, consumer responses are defined, legacy writers are fenced, and every accepted source change reaches the destination. Required synchronous Catalog assessments can interrupt new orders during a Catalog failure, and projections reduce that dependency only for operations covered by their freshness contract.
Signal and evaluation window & Affected operations, shared resource use, and independent rollback results, measured during isolation and migration rehearsals.
Control and decision & Transfer write authority only after source writers are stopped, active transactions are resolved, final changes are applied, and verification passes. Judge the extraction by the release and failure dependencies it was meant to remove.
Owner and review trigger & Catalog owns its migrations and recovery, consumer teams own their integrations and unavailable responses, and product owners resolve eligibility and freshness requirements that affect order acceptance. Review after any change that requires coordinated releases, and before the next extraction.
:::
